title: 2 Samuel 20:4–13
context: David orders Amasa to muster Judah within three days, and when Amasa delays, David sends Abishai with the king’s forces, including Joab’s men, the Cherethites, and the Pelethites, to pursue Sheba before he can reach fortified cities. At the great stone in Gibeon, Joab greets Amasa as his brother and kills him with a sword while seeming to kiss him, recalling Joab’s earlier killing of Abner (2 Samuel 3:27). The Hebrew of verse 8 does not make clear how the falling sword relates to the attack, and interpreters offer different explanations. The narrator reports the deed without approval, and David later describes Joab as having shed the blood of war in peace (1 Kings 2:5). Readers in both traditions commonly treat this as a sober account of ambition and violence, not a model to follow.

verses.text: Then the king said to Amasa, “Call me the men of Judah together within three days, and be here present.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David ordering Amasa to gather the men of Judah within three days. The new commander is given his first task.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the order as fulfilling David’s earlier promise to Amasa (2 Samuel 19:13). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a test of Amasa’s leadership.

verses.text: So Amasa went to call the men of Judah together, but he stayed longer than the set time which had been appointed to him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Amasa stayed longer than the set time. The delay creates danger, since Sheba’s revolt gains time while the muster lags.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the delay as the occasion for what follows, though the text does not explain its cause. Readers in both traditions commonly avoid guessing at Amasa’s reasons.

verses.text: David said to Abishai, “Now Sheba the son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom did. Take your lord’s servants and pursue after him, lest he get himself fortified cities, and escape out of our sight.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David sending Abishai after Sheba, warning that Sheba could do more harm than Absalom. Urgency drives the response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David’s concern for the kingdom’s stability. Both traditions commonly read the verse as wise awareness of the threat.

verses.text: Joab’s men went out after him with the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the mighty men; and they went out of Jerusalem to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Joab’s men, the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and the mighty men going out to pursue Sheba. The king’s forces respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Joab’s men are prominent, hinting that Joab remains a powerful figure. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as setting the stage for the encounter with Amasa.

verses.text: When they were at the great stone which is in Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Joab was clothed in his apparel of war that he had put on, and on it was a sash with a sword fastened on his waist in its sheath; and as he went along it fell out.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Amasa meeting Joab at the great stone in Gibeon, while Joab is armed in his war apparel. The scene is tense.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the detail of the sword as preparing for Joab’s treachery. Both traditions commonly read the verse without speculating beyond what the text says about the weapon.

verses.text: Joab said to Amasa, “Is it well with you, my brother?” Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Joab greeting Amasa as his brother and taking his beard to kiss him. Friendly words mask a deadly intent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the false kiss as a picture of betrayal (compare Proverbs 27:6), and some readers in both traditions recall the betrayal of Jesus with a kiss (Luke 22:48). Both traditions commonly hold that connection loosely.

verses.text: But Amasa took no heed to the sword that was in Joab’s hand. So he struck him with it in the body and shed out his bowels to the ground, and didn’t strike him again; and he died. Joab and Abishai his brother pursued Sheba the son of Bichri.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Amasa not noticing the sword and Joab killing him with one stroke before pursuing Sheba. The narrator reports the deed plainly without approving it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the murder as another instance of Joab’s violence, which David later describes as shedding the blood of war in peace (1 Kings 2:5). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, as a warning rather than a model.

verses.text: One of Joab’s young men stood by him, and said, “He who favors Joab, and he who is for David, let him follow Joab!”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see one of Joab’s men calling those who favor Joab and David to follow him. Loyalty is claimed in the shadow of murder.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the call as an attempt to rally support for Joab despite his crime. Both traditions commonly see the irony of linking loyalty to David with Joab’s violent act.

verses.text: Amasa lay wallowing in his blood in the middle of the highway. When the man saw that all the people stood still, he carried Amasa out of the highway into the field, and cast a garment over him when he saw that everyone who came by him stood still.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Amasa lying in the highway, causing the people to stop, until he is moved to a field and covered. Death has halted the march.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the people’s pause as a moment of shock and conscience. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse with restraint, noting the human cost of ambition.

verses.text: When he was removed out of the highway, all the people went on after Joab to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people going on after Joab once Amasa is removed. The pursuit continues as though nothing happened.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the swift return to the chase as showing how violence can be overlooked for the sake of victory. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober comment on Joab’s power.
